title: Inheritance, interfaces, traits
summary: Extend a class, promise a contract with interfaces, share bodies with traits.

blocks.html:
class ReportCard extends GradeCalculator says a report card is a calculator: it has every public method the parent has, and may add more. honors() is one line of new behavior on top of the grade the parent already computes.

If the child declares its own constructor, it must pass the arguments up with parent::__construct(...). The parent's properties are set there and nowhere else.

blocks.title: a report card is a grade calculator
blocks.code:
<?php

use App\GradeCalculator;

class ReportCard extends GradeCalculator
{
    public function __construct(
        float $quiz,
        float $assignment,
        float $midterm,
        float $final,
    ) {
        parent::__construct($quiz, $assignment, $midterm, $final);
    }

    public function honors(): bool
    {
        return $this->getFinalGrade() >= 90;
    }
}

$card = new ReportCard(90.0, 92.0, 88.0, 95.0);

echo $card->getFinalGrade(), ' ', $card->getLetterGrade(), "\n";
echo ($card->honors() ? 'with honors' : 'no honors'), "\n";

blocks.html: Skip that parent::__construct() call and the object still builds, quietly. The parent's readonly properties are never assigned, so the first inherited method that reads one throws Error: Typed property GradeCalculator::$quiz must not be accessed before initialization. Every child constructor forwards to its parent.

An abstract class cannot be instantiated. It exists so that children can be: it mixes finished methods with abstract ones — a signature and a return type, no body. Every concrete child must supply the body, so calling headline() on any report is safe even though the abstract class never wrote it.

A child may also replace an inherited method entirely. That is overriding, and parent::describe() reaches the version it replaced.

blocks.title: abstract method, concrete child, overridden method
blocks.code:
<?php

abstract class Report
{
    abstract public function headline(): string;

    public function describe(): string
    {
        return 'a report';
    }
}

class TermReport extends Report
{
    public function __construct(private readonly string $term) {}

    public function headline(): string
    {
        return 'Term ' . $this->term;
    }

    public function describe(): string
    {
        return parent::describe() . ' for ' . $this->headline();
    }
}

$report = new TermReport('2nd');

echo $report->describe(), "\n";

blocks.html:
An interface is a contract with no state: method signatures and nothing to inherit. A class implements it and promises the bodies. Unlike a parent class, a class may implement as many interfaces as it likes, which is how unrelated types share a capability — printable, comparable, countable.

The interface is what a caller programs against. If a page only needs summarize(), it does not care whether the object is a quiz or a report.

blocks.title: two interfaces, one class
blocks.code:
<?php

interface Printable
{
    public function summarize(): string;
}

interface Scored
{
    public function score(): float;
}

class Quiz implements Printable, Scored
{
    public function __construct(private readonly float $points) {}

    public function score(): float
    {
        return $this->points;
    }

    public function summarize(): string
    {
        return 'Quiz worth ' . $this->points . ' points';
    }
}

$quiz = new Quiz(88.5);

echo $quiz->summarize(), "\n";
echo $quiz->score(), "\n";

blocks.html: A trait is a bundle of finished method bodies that you drop into a class with use. It is not a type, it cannot be instantiated, and PHP copies the methods in as if you had typed them in the class yourself. Reach for a trait when several unrelated classes need the same code — inheritance is for one family, a trait is for a habit.

blocks.title: a trait for stamping
blocks.code:
<?php

trait Timestampable
{
    private ?string $stamp = null;

    public function stampOn(string $date): void
    {
        $this->stamp = $date;
    }

    public function stamp(): string
    {
        return $this->stamp ?? 'not stamped';
    }
}

class Quiz
{
    use Timestampable;

    public function __construct(private readonly float $points) {}
}

$quiz = new Quiz(88.5);

echo $quiz->stamp(), "\n";
$quiz->stampOn('2024-06-14');
echo $quiz->stamp(), "\n";

blocks.html:
final closes a door: on a method it makes overriding a fatal error, on a class it makes extending one. Use it wherever a subclass changing that behavior would be a bug, such as a constructor that sets an invariant.

And keep the ordering in mind: inheritance is for a genuine is-a. When a class merely uses another, hold an instance in a property and call it — composition — because two small classes that call each other stay free to change, while a parent and its children are welded together. Reach for extends last, not first.

blocks.title: what final refuses
blocks.code:
<?php

class Report
{
    final public function describe(): string
    {
        return 'a report';
    }
}

class TermReport extends Report
{
    public function describe(): string
    {
        return 'overridden';
    }
}

// Fatal error: Cannot override final method Report::describe()

blocks.title: all three at once: extends, implements, use
blocks.code:
<?php

use App\GradeCalculator;

trait Timestampable
{
    private ?string $stamp = null;

    public function stampOn(string $date): void
    {
        $this->stamp = $date;
    }

    public function stamp(): string
    {
        return $this->stamp ?? 'not stamped';
    }
}

interface Printable
{
    public function summarize(): string;
}

class ReportCard extends GradeCalculator implements Printable
{
    use Timestampable;

    public function honors(): bool
    {
        return $this->getFinalGrade() >= 90;
    }

    public function summarize(): string
    {
        return $this->getLetterGrade()
            . ' (' . number_format($this->getFinalGrade(), 2) . ')'
            . ', stamped ' . $this->stamp();
    }
}

$card = new ReportCard(90.0, 92.0, 88.0, 95.0);
$card->stampOn('2024-06-14');

echo $card->summarize(), "\n";
echo ($card->honors() ? 'honors' : 'no honors'), "\n";

quiz.q: A child class declares its own __construct(). What does it owe the parent?
options: A parent::__construct(...) call with the arguments it was given
It must repeat the parent's property declarations
quiz.why: The parent's constructor is the only place its promoted properties are assigned. Without the parent:: call the object exists but its inherited state was never initialized, and the first method that reads it throws an Error.

quiz.q: How many interfaces may one class implement?
quiz.why: Interface lists are comma-separated: class Quiz implements Printable, Scored. A class has a single parent, but capabilities stack.

quiz.q: What does final on a method do?
options: Makes overriding it a fatal error
Prevents the class from being instantiated
quiz.why: final marks a method as complete: a child that tries to redeclare it stops the script with Cannot override final method. Writing final on the class instead blocks extending it.

exercise.brief: Combine the three pieces. A trait Named whose method name(): string returns $this->name. An abstract class Report with an abstract headline(): string and a concrete banner(): string returning '== ' . headline() . ' =='. A class TermReport extends Report, uses Named, promotes a readonly string $name, and returns 'Term ' . $this->name from headline(). Print the banner for the name 2nd.
exercise.starter:
<?php

// trait, abstract class, child class, one echo
exercise.hint: A trait is pulled in with use Named; inside the class body, on the same level as the property and the methods. banner() lives in the parent and calls the abstract method, so the child only writes headline().
exercise.solution:
<?php

trait Named
{
    public function name(): string
    {
        return $this->name;
    }
}

abstract class Report
{
    abstract public function headline(): string;

    public function banner(): string
    {
        return '== ' . $this->headline() . ' ==';
    }
}

class TermReport extends Report
{
    use Named;

    public function __construct(private readonly string $name) {}

    public function headline(): string
    {
        return 'Term ' . $this->name;
    }
}

$report = new TermReport('2nd');

echo $report->banner(), "\n";
